analysis.one_liner: Cancels up to $25,000 of federal student loan debt for every borrower, tax-free.
analysis.headline: A bill to cancel up to $25,000 of student loan debt per borrower was introduced in the House in February 2022, referred to two committees, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Department of Education to cancel or pay off up to $25,000 of federal student loan debt for every borrower — covering unpaid principal, interest, and fees — and made sure borrowers wouldn't owe income tax on the forgiven amount. It was introduced by one representative, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Every borrower with outstanding federal student loans would have up to $25,000 erased — including private, state, and local government workers whose loans the bill covers even though those loans are not held by the Education Department. Borrowers would save the monthly payments and interest on that debt, and would not owe taxes on the cancelled amount.

how_it_helps.text: Within 90 days of enactment, the Education Department would have to cancel or pay off up to $25,000 of each borrower's federal student loans, including unpaid principal, accrued interest, and fees.
The cancelled amount would not count as taxable income, so borrowers would not owe a tax bill on the relief.
Payments would go first to the borrower's highest-interest loans, and borrowers with larger total balances could get relief on up to $25,000 of them.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the federal budget, would fund the cancellation — including repaying private lenders and guarantee agencies that hold federally backed loans, which the bill defines as eligible for repayment.

drawbacks.text: The government (taxpayers) would bear the cost of erasing up to $25,000 per borrower, including repaying private banks and guarantee agencies that hold federally backed loans, a cost the bill does not offset with new revenue.
The relief is not limited by income: a high-earning borrower and a low-wage worker would each receive the same $25,000, so part of the spending goes to those who need it least.
The bill addresses existing debt only; it does nothing to reduce the cost of college or new borrowing, which critics of broad forgiveness point to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — up to $25,000 in debt wiped out for every borrower, tax-free — is large and straightforward. The costs an honest supporter would acknowledge: the federal government (taxpayers) absorbs the erased balances, including repaying private holders of guaranteed loans, and the benefit is not targeted by income, so higher-earning borrowers with larger balances would also receive relief. Critics also argued broad forgiveness does nothing to lower the cost of college going forward. As a one-chamber bill with no cosponsors, it never got far enough for those tradeoffs to be weighed in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the two House committees it was referred to and was never voted on before the term ended.

narrative.text: Representative Vicente Gonzalez introduced the Student Loan Relief Act in the House on February 11, 2022.
It was referred to the Education and Labor Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day; neither committee took it up.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never reached the House floor.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan borrowers remain in debt as before; the lending and servicing industry keeps its existing loan books and revenue, and no one else gained from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders and servicers kept their loan books

for.name: Rep. Vicente Gonzalez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the Education Department to cancel up to $25,000 of each borrower's federal student loans.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never took action on the bill after its referral.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor; with no committee action and no cosponsors, leadership never scheduled it for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of the support was never tested.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and collection companies
industries.note: A $25,000-per-borrower wipeout would shrink the balances they service and the volume of loans in repayment and collections, reducing fee and interest revenue. Ordinary borrowers' gain comes directly out of this revenue stream.

industries.industry: Private holders of federally guaranteed student loans (banks and guarantee agencies)
industries.note: The bill covers loans made, insured, or guaranteed under the Higher Education Act even when not held by the Education Department; those holders would be repaid by the government and would exit a profitable loan book. Their interest in continuing to collect from borrowers ran against the relief borrowers would receive.
